text: You rerun your analysis. The tables update. The numbers in your paper don't.
A results section can hold hundreds of numbers typed by hand. One stale value, a sign that flips, a p-value that crosses point zero five, and the text no longer says what the data say.
provenum ties every number to the table cell that produced it. Instead of typing fifty-three point zero, you write a reference. Rerun the analysis, and the text follows.

Converting an existing paper is the hard part. Our test paper has three hundred and seven numbers, and most of them match more than one cell. So a local language model proposes the cell each sentence means, and the code accepts it only if the value reproduces exactly what you wrote.
In the app, you upload your Overleaf project and your result tables. provenum works out how each table is laid out, finds every number, and asks the model.
Then you review. Where several cells share a value, you confirm the choice, because a value check alone cannot tell them apart. Nothing changes until you apply.

On our test paper, the model's suggestions linked two hundred and forty-nine numbers. Two hundred and twenty-eight match the hand-checked version, and twenty of the other twenty-one were in the list you confirm. And the PDF reads exactly the same.
After the next rerun, provenum diff lists the sentences whose numbers changed, and flags the claims that broke.
Your manuscript stays on your machine, and the model runs locally. provenum. Numbers you can trace.
